name: Lupine Science
mission: Make AI predictions of new materials checkable before a lab commits to them.
oneLiner: Lupine Science measures where machine-learned models of atoms go wrong, against published references and pass/fail gates set in advance, and publishes every verdict, failures included.
description: Lupine Science is an early-stage, founder-led research company. We independently measure the errors of machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), test corrections against preregistered gates, record any amendment made after results are seen, and publish the verdict: pass, fail or abstain. Correction is a research question here, not a product: it has held only in narrow, stated cases. Nothing we have published is peer-reviewed yet.
contactLine: Research partners, model builders, press and investors
knowsAbout: Benchmarking foundation models for atomistic simulation
Elastic and surface properties of metals

licence.text: You can reuse our code (MIT) and our first-party text and data (CC BY 4.0) with attribution and no share-alike obligations.

highlights.title: A blind prediction held
highlights.text: For nine fcc metals, an error field fitted to three other properties predicted the never-fitted (110) surface-energy error of four foundation models, significantly for three of the four.

highlights.title: A correction ceiling, not a fix
highlights.text: On 16 cubic metals, an elastic-constant correction helped only when the held-out answer set how far to correct. One that works without seeing the answer is still open.

highlights.title: Round 4: no gate passed
highlights.text: In July 2026, migration barriers, a lattice and elastic correction, and a catalyst correction failed. Magnetism abstained: no available model had the spin physics it needed.

tested.scope: Nine fcc metals, four foundation MLIPs: a field fitted to three other observables predicted the never-fitted (110) error at r = 0.906 across 36 cells (material-clustered 95% CI 0.82–0.96; permutation null near 0.44; significant for three of the four models).
Blind (110) surface-energy error fell from 9.7% to 1.5% on nickel and from 28.0% to 13.7% on copper: one model, two metals, one facet.
Across 21 materials and 228 published reference values, four foundation MLIPs ranked surface energies almost correctly (Spearman 0.88–1.00) while missing magnitudes by tens of percent.

tested.what: Shared error direction across models (21 materials)
tested.scope: Apparent cross-model alignment sat inside a coupling-aware null, so we do not count it as a result.

Four MatPES MLIPs, 128 cases, approximate r2SCAN targets: one bias direction per functional transfers out of sample. Sized by the held-out reference, MAE falls 17.84 → 10.36 GPa: a ceiling, not a deployable correction. Blind correction open; derived moduli uncertified.
On the same 16-metal panel, 1×1×1 TensorNet/PBE cells matched 3×3×3 cells for elastic-constant error (14.55 vs 14.61 GPa MAE).

tested.what: Global elastic correction on that panel
tested.scope: A global correction made the result worse: 63.40 GPa MAE.
On CoCrNi and CoCrFeNi, a correction learned on elemental fcc metals made median bulk-modulus error worse: 9.1% to 16.9%.
30-path panel; MACE-MP-0 small and medium, MACE-MPA-0 medium and CHGNet missed a 40 meV gate (MAE 135.0–242.5 meV on completed paths).
Rocksalt ionics and perovskites: ionics 0/4; perovskites 0/1 after a post-measurement amendment.
Every selected Δ-correction made holdout error worse.
No available model had the spin physics the test needed.
Four of seven registered predictions across two experiments failed. The 90% conformal intervals reached 86.7% coverage, below the registered 90%.
On the 30-path Li-ion panel, fitted on 12 disjoint training paths: all four models abstained at the direction gate, so no correction was applied.

Preregistered 40 meV gate against published VASP barriers failed on path 7 (118.8 meV). A post-failure amendment moved the gate to a same-engine check, which passed; against published references the error was 693.0–705.7 meV. Same-engine only.

resultNotes: Not a gated test: in an [October 2026 retrospective](/articles/what-error-patterns-can-tell-us/) of previously examined data, errors stayed concentrated, but a learned shared direction added little or no advantage over a common-direction baseline. No new physical validation is claimed.

cannotClaim.text: That any correction we have tested is ready to deploy. In Round 4 (July 2026) no gate passed, and the 16-metal elastic result is a ceiling that needs the held-out answer.
That different models share one error direction on surface energies. In our 21-material benchmark, apparent alignment sat inside a coupling-aware null.
That a Lean check confirms the physics.
Anything about the newest multi-head or multi-fidelity models or their confidence heads. We have not tested them.
Peer review. No Lupine paper has been peer-reviewed or accepted yet.

lean.example: One example, from the blind surface-energy test: at the 10⁻⁴ precision used for checking, one cell’s improvement rounds to zero, so we report 26 of 36 (27 of 36 at float64).

items: Gates first: we write the pass/fail gate before a test runs, label any amendment made after results are seen, and publish the data, the gate and the verdict together: pass, fail or abstain.
Founder-led, with AI coding and research agents working under rules that live in code. AI assistance is disclosed, and a human author is responsible for every public summary.
Key-person risk is real: the program depends on one founder. Public data, code and the failure ledger mean the results can be checked without us.
howWeWork.linkText: How we use AI agents and handle data: the rules, how far each reaches, and where data goes

faq.a: No Lupine paper has been peer-reviewed or accepted yet. The TMS2027 poster is a conference presentation, not a paper. Each article carries a status label and links the data it uses.

faq.q: Will newer multi-head models, with their own uncertainty estimates, make this unnecessary?
faq.a: They may change what needs testing, and we have not tested them yet. A model’s own uncertainty still needs an outside, preregistered check against published references: models trained on similar data can agree and still be wrong. If you build one, we would like to test it.

Yes. You can reuse our code (MIT) and our first-party text and data (CC BY 4.0) with attribution and no share-alike obligations; third-party material keeps its own terms. The data is in [lupine-rhizo](https://github.com/alexwelcing/lupine-rhizo).

The accepted abstract described a universal error 'hyper-ribbon'; our record no longer supports that, and the proceedings manuscript replaces it with narrower measurement claims.
